title: The Vanguard of Migration (in the Cause of Allah)

topics.title: The Vanguard of Migration (in the Cause of Allah)

paragraphs.text: After the endorsement of the Second 'Aqabah Pledge and the establishment of a small Muslim state in a vast desert surging with disbelief and ignorance — the most serious gain in terms of Islam — the Prophet (Peace be upon him) gave his leave for the Muslims to migrate to Madinah, the nascent Muslim state. Migration to Madinah, in terms of personal interests, was no more than material waste and sacrifice of wealth, all in return for personal safety only. Even here, the migrant could not expect full security; he was liable to be robbed or even killed. The future was foggy, pregnant with various unpredictable sorrows and crises.

Bearing all this in mind, the Muslims began to migrate, while the polytheists spared no effort in hindering and debarring them. The first one to migrate was Abu Salamah, a year before the Great 'Aqabah Pledge. When he had made up his mind to leave Makkah, his in-laws detained his wife and snatched his son, dislocating the boy's hand. Umm Salamah, after the departure of her husband and the loss of her son, spent a year weeping and lamenting. A relative eventually had pity on her and the others released her son; she then set out on a 500-kilometre journey with no help, until at a spot called At-Tan'im, 'Uthman bin Talhah came across her and gave her and her son a ride, and she joined Abu Salamah in the village of Quba'.

Another instance was Suhaib. When he expressed his wish to migrate, the disbelievers insulted him, claiming he had come into Makkah a worthless tramp and become wealthy only thanks to them, and ordered that he would not leave. He offered to give away all his wealth to them, and they agreed to release him on that condition. The Prophet (Peace be upon him) heard this and commented: "Suhaib is the winner, after all."

Then there was the story of 'Umar bin Al-Khattab, 'Ayyash bin Abi Rabi'a and Hisham bin Al-'Asi, who agreed to meet one morning to leave for Madinah; 'Umar and 'Ayyash came, but Hisham was detained. Shortly afterwards Abu Jahl and his brother Al-Harith came to Madinah to see their brother 'Ayyash, claiming his mother had sworn she would never comb her hair nor shade herself from the sun until she had seen him. 'Ayyash took pity, but 'Umar warned him it was a trick to entice him from Islam, adding, "your mother would comb her hair if lice pestered her, and would shade herself if the sun got too hot." 'Ayyash insisted on going; 'Umar gave him his docile camel, advising him to flee on it if he sensed treachery. On the way, Abu Jahl feigned trouble with his own camel and asked to ride behind 'Ayyash; when they knelt down, the two polytheists fell upon 'Ayyash, tied him, and rode into Makkah shouting at people to deal likewise with their 'fools'.

These are three self-explanatory models of the Makkans' reaction towards anyone intending to migrate. Nevertheless, the believers still managed to escape in successive groups, so rapidly that within two months of the Second 'Aqabah Pledge, entire quarters of Makkah were deserted. Almost all the followers of Muhammad (Peace be upon him) had migrated, except Abu Bakr, 'Ali, the Prophet (Peace be upon him) himself, and those helpless souls who had been detained or were unable to escape. Most of the Muslims who had migrated to Abyssinia (Ethiopia) also came back to Madinah to join the rest.

The situation was critical in Makkah, but Muhammad (Peace be upon him) was not perturbed. Abu Bakr was urging the Prophet to depart and was eagerly waiting to accompany him on this eventful journey, but the Prophet told him that the time had not yet come and the Lord had not given him the command to migrate. In anticipation of Allah's Command, Abu Bakr had purchased two swift camels and fed them properly for four months so that they could withstand the ordeals of the long desert journey.

topics.topicSummary: After the Second 'Aqabah Pledge, the Prophet ﷺ permitted the Muslims to migrate to Madinah — a sacrifice of wealth and safety into an uncertain future. The polytheists tried to hinder them: Abu Salamah's family tore him from his wife and son; Suhaib bought his freedom with all his wealth ('Suhaib is the winner'); and 'Ayyash was tricked and captured. Yet the believers escaped in waves until Makkah's quarters emptied, leaving only Abu Bakr, 'Ali, the Prophet ﷺ, and the helpless — while Abu Bakr readied two camels and awaited the command to depart.
